**Attaching it to `weave.Evaluation`**

Weave takes Scorers as arguments to a `weave.Evaluation`. A function-based Scorer is a Python function decorated with `@weave.op`, and it must return a dictionary [S1]. You put it in the `scorers` list [S2].

In the tutorial, Weave expects a `target` to compare `output` against, and its example scorer takes arguments named `target` and `output` [S3]. Your `expected` argument name may therefore need to match your dataset's column. I haven't read the `column_map` section, so check it if the names differ.

```python
import asyncio
import weave

@weave.op()
def exact_match(expected: str, output: str) -> dict:
    return {'correct': output == expected}

weave.init('my_project')  # placeholder project name

evaluation = weave.Evaluation(
    name='exact_match_eval',
    dataset=dataset,   # placeholder: your dataset, defined elsewhere
    scorers=[exact_match],
)
print(asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(model)))  # placeholder: your model
```

In a Python script, use `asyncio.run`. In a Jupyter notebook, use `await evaluation.evaluate(model)` directly [S2].

sources.text:
## Create your own scorers

Custom Scorers let you encode evaluation criteria that are specific to your use case, beyond what the built-in Scorers cover. The following sections describe the two ways to define a Scorer: as a function, or as a class for more complex logic.

> [!TIP]
>
> **Ready-to-use scorers**
> Although this guide shows you how to create custom scorers, Weave comes with [predefined scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md) and [local SLM scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/weave_local_scorers.md) that you can use right away, including:
>
> * [Hallucination detection](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md#hallucinationfreescorer)
> * [Summarization quality](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md#summarizationscorer)
> * [Embedding similarity](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md#embeddingsimilarityscorer)
> * [Toxicity detection (local)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/weave_local_scorers.md#weavetoxicityscorerv1)
> * [Context relevance scoring (local)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/weave_local_scorers.md#weavecontextrelevancescorerv1)

# Scoring overview

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

This guide is for developers who want to measure the quality of their AI system's outputs. It explains how Scorers fit into Weave evaluations, how to build your own Scorers, how to apply Scorers to individual calls, and how to analyze the resulting scores.

**Python**

Pass Scorers to a `weave.Evaluation` object during evaluation. Weave supports two types of Scorers:

1. **Function-based Scorers:** Python functions decorated with `@weave.op`.
2. **Class-based Scorers:** Python classes that inherit from `weave.Scorer` for more complex evaluations.

Scorers must return a dictionary and can return multiple metrics, nested metrics, and non-numeric values such as text returned from an LLM-evaluator about its reasoning.

**TypeScript**

Scorers are special ops that you pass to a `weave.Evaluation` object during evaluation.

## Use a built-in scorer and run the evaluation

With the model, dataset, and a custom scorer in place, you're ready to wire everything together into an evaluation run.

Along with custom scoring functions, you can also use [Weave's built-in scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md). In the following evaluation, `weave.Evaluation()` uses the `fruit_name_score` function defined in the previous section and the built-in `MultiTaskBinaryClassificationF1` scorer, which computes [F1 scores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-score).

The following example runs an evaluation of `ExtractFruitsModel` on the `fruits` dataset using the two scoring functions and logs the results to Weave.

**Python**

```python lines {3-10} theme={"system"}
weave.init('eval_pipeline_quickstart')

evaluation = weave.Evaluation(
    name='fruit_eval',
    dataset=dataset, 
    scorers=[
        MultiTaskBinaryClassificationF1(class_names=["fruit", "color", "flavor"]), 
        fruit_name_score
    ],
)
print(asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(model)))

> Use Weave's predefined scorers for evaluating your AI applications

Weave offers several predefined scorers for evaluating your AI applications, such as [Hallucination detection](#hallucinationfreescorer) and [Summarization quality](#summarizationscorer). These can help you quickly define an evaluation and score your application's outputs. This page describes each built-in scorer, what it measures, and how to use it in an evaluation.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Local scorers are only available for the Weave Python SDK. They aren't yet available for the Weave TypeScript SDK.
>
> To use Weave scorers in TypeScript, see [function-based scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md#function-based-scorers).

results.snippet:
## How Weave guardrails work

Weave guardrails use inline [Weave Scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md) to assess the input from a user or the output from an LLM and adjust the LLM's responses in real time. You can configure custom scorers or use [built-in scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md) to assess content for a variety of purposes. This guide demonstrates how to use both types of scorers as guardrails.

If you want to passively score production traffic without modifying your application's control flow, use [monitors](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md) instead.

Unlike monitors, guardrails require code changes because they affect your application's control flow. However, every scorer result from guardrails is automatically stored in Weave's database, so your guardrails also function as monitors without any extra configuration. You can analyze historical scorer results regardless of how they were originally used.

## Create your own scorers

Custom Scorers let you encode evaluation criteria that are specific to your use case, beyond what the built-in Scorers cover. The following sections describe the two ways to define a Scorer: as a function, or as a class for more complex logic.

> [!TIP]
>
> **Ready-to-use scorers**
> Although this guide shows you how to create custom scorers, Weave comes with [predefined scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md) and [local SLM scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/weave_local_scorers.md) that you can use right away, including:
>
> * [Hallucination detection](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md#hallucinationfreescorer)
> * [Summarization quality](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md#summarizationscorer)
> * [Embedding similarity](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/builtin_scorers.md#embeddingsimilarityscorer)
> * [Toxicity detection (local)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/weave_local_scorers.md#weavetoxicityscorerv1)
> * [Context relevance scoring (local)](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/weave_local_scorers.md#weavecontextrelevancescorerv1)

# Scoring overview

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

This guide is for developers who want to measure the quality of their AI system's outputs. It explains how Scorers fit into Weave evaluations, how to build your own Scorers, how to apply Scorers to individual calls, and how to analyze the resulting scores.

**Python**

Pass Scorers to a `weave.Evaluation` object during evaluation. Weave supports two types of Scorers:

1. **Function-based Scorers:** Python functions decorated with `@weave.op`.
2. **Class-based Scorers:** Python classes that inherit from `weave.Scorer` for more complex evaluations.

Scorers must return a dictionary and can return multiple metrics, nested metrics, and non-numeric values such as text returned from an LLM-evaluator about its reasoning.

**TypeScript**

Scorers are special ops that you pass to a `weave.Evaluation` object during evaluation.

# Build an evaluation

> Learn how to build an evaluation pipeline with Weave Models and Evaluations

[Try in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/tutorial-eval.ipynb)

[GitHub source](https://github.com/wandb/examples/blob/main/colabs/weave/tutorial-eval.ipynb)

This tutorial walks you through building an end-to-end evaluation pipeline in Weave so you can measure and track the quality of an LLM application as you iterate on it. Evaluations help you compare changes against a consistent set of examples and detect regressions before they reach users. This tutorial targets developers who build LLM-powered applications and want a repeatable way to test them.

Weave provides built-in support for tracking evaluations with [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) and [`Evaluation`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/evaluations) classes. The APIs make minimal assumptions, so they fit a range of use cases.

**Attaching it to `weave.Evaluation`**

Weave takes Scorers as arguments to a `weave.Evaluation`. A function-based Scorer is a Python function decorated with `@weave.op`, and it must return a dictionary [S1]. You put it in the `scorers` list [S2].

```python
import asyncio
import weave

@weave.op()
def exact_match(expected: str, output: str) -> dict:
    return {'correct': output == expected}

weave.init('my_project')  # placeholder project name

evaluation = weave.Evaluation(
    name='exact_match_eval',
    dataset=dataset,   # placeholder: your dataset, defined elsewhere
    scorers=[exact_match],
)
print(asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(model)))  # placeholder: your model
```

In a Python script, use `asyncio.run`. In a Jupyter notebook, use `await evaluation.evaluate(model)` directly [S2].

`dataset` and `model` are placeholders for objects you define yourself. I haven't run the Weave part of this example.
